title: -7 // 2 is -4 and -7 % 2 is 1 in Python, but Math.trunc(-7 / 2) is -3 and -7 % 2 is -1 in JavaScript
assumption: Integer division of a negative number by a positive one rounds the same way in every language -- toward zero.

input.description: Any pagination, bucketing, or hashing logic computed with integer division or modulo on a value that can be negative -- e.g. 'which page is item index i on' or 'which bucket does this signed offset fall into'.

what_goes_wrong: The same division expression applied to a negative dividend gives a different quotient AND a different-signed remainder depending on the language, so a bucketing or pagination formula ported between a Python backend and a JS frontend (or vice versa) silently puts negative-offset items in a different bucket on each side.
why: Python's `//` is floor division: it rounds the mathematical quotient toward negative infinity, so -7 // 2 = -4 (since -3.5 floors to -4), and `%` is defined to satisfy `a == (a // b) * b + a % b`, which forces the remainder to take the sign of the divisor, giving -7 % 2 = 1. JavaScript's `/` followed by `Math.trunc` (or the legacy `~~`/`|0` truncation idioms) rounds toward zero instead, so -7/2 truncates to -3, and `%` in JS is a remainder operation (not a true modulo) that takes the sign of the DIVIDEND, giving -7 % 2 = -1. (JavaScript's `/` itself returns -3.5; `Math.floor(-7 / 2)` gives -4 and matches Python's `//`, so the quotient only diverges if you truncate. The `%` sign difference is built into the operator.)
fix: Never port a division/modulo-based formula between Python and JavaScript without checking the sign convention explicitly; if you need Python's floor-mod behavior in JS, write it out as `((a % b) + b) % b` rather than relying on `%` alone.
